title: What is known about 1RB0LB_0RC0LF_1LD1RE_0LA0RB_0RD0RF_0LA---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LB_0RC0LF_1LD1RE_0LA0RB_0RD0RF_0LA---.
intro: This six-state machine is a holdout of the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on: the structure of its run (two counters ticking together), the rules proved in Lean, and the open question.
verdict: The question is open. The machine is a rewriting system on the right half of its tape (the visit law, proved in Lean): it halts only if a visit meets 111. Its first four rules are those of the three machines that busycoq PR59 proves to halt in round 161,211 on the block 1011; this machine rewrites 1011 to 0001 instead and, in an accelerated run (computed, not proved), carries on: no halt up to round 5,000,000. No halt in the first 1011 steps of a direct run. The only junk a word can hold is 11, made when a count runs out with one visit just before a 1 at the word end; there have been 21 in 5,000,000 rounds, all harmless, and one would be dangerous only if the deficit of the count entering its last digit block were odd (in the deficit form of lean/Deficit.lean).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The sweeps of the run
claims.text: The shift rules the machine uses in its run (every sweep met when the symbolic simulator runs from many configurations of the run), each for every number of copies.

claims.title: Both counters' increments, for all sizes
claims.text: At an event (A on cell 3), the same 9 theorems as the reference 1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_0RD1RB_0RC--- (proved here again for this machine): At an event (A on cell 3): the left increment with a carry over n ones (12n+24 steps), the right increment on a lowest 0 (28 steps) and with a carry over k+1 ones three cells apart (8k+36 steps), with the engine block plain or marked, and carries crossing junk units 1010000, which they leave unchanged (one unit; j units in a row, 24j+36 steps; j units and then k+1 more ones, 24j+8k+44 steps). Plus y_e1_detour: L E> 1 0 R reaches L 1 B> 0 R in 3 steps (E1 = 0RF, F0 = 0LA, A0 = 1RB), where the reference's E1 = 1RB takes 1.

claims.title: The visit law: the machine as a rewriting system
claims.text: A visit (the head enters a stream s in state C with a 0 on its left and returns in state A two cells further left) rewrites the stream by 0 s → 1 s, 100 s → 000 v(s), 110 s → 000 v(s), 1010 s → 1010 v(v(s)), 1011 s → 0001 s, for every stream and every tape to the left. 111 s halts the machine. The six prefixes 0, 100, 110, 111, 1010 and 1011 cover every stream, so these rules are the whole machine: it can halt only when a visit meets 111. From blank tape the run is a sequence of rounds 0∞ A> 1 0 S → 0∞ A> 1 0 v(1 0 S), starting from S = 1 0∞ after 4 steps.

claims.title: The word computation is the machine
claims.text: A computable pass over the word (exact counts, one block at a time) gives the tape after every round; if it reports a halt the machine halts, and if every number of rounds computes to a word the machine never halts. After a junk event, a round entering at offset 1 is harmless (through 1011), and one entering at offset 2 halts the machine.

claims.title: The first 2,000 rounds
claims.text: The word computation runs through the first 2,000 rounds (about 10<sup>300</sup> visits) without a halt, checked by evaluation.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 252 cells have been visited and 74 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: A direct run of 1011 steps (longrun.c, the simulator of tools/c/tm.h) without a halt.

claims.title: The left side is clockwork
claims.text: Between consecutive left-end extensions the busiest cell turns exactly 2<sup>k</sup> times, each power twice (64, 64, 128, 128, ..., 2<sup>24</sup>), in the first 1.5·10<sup>9</sup> steps.

claims.title: E1 is rare
claims.text: E1 is used 306 times in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps; every other non-halting transition 10<sup>7</sup> to 2·10<sup>8</sup> times.

claims.title: How much of the run the increments cover
claims.text: In the first 108 steps (1,048,574 events) 95.2% of the events are instances of these theorems (left 524,258; right0 262,133; right1 92,325; junk_10 78,635; junk_110 39,313; junk_jk 1,733; right1m 9; right0m 1). The other 50,167 are carries over junk layouts the rules do not list (two junk stretches, junk words other than 1010000) and the moments around left-end visits. The event tapes are the reference's (first 2,000,000 events compared); each event comes 2 steps later per earlier use of E1 (498 = 2 × 249).

claims.title: It does not halt where the PR59 machines halt
claims.text: The first four rules are also the rules of the three machines that busycoq PR59 proves to halt (they halt on 1011, in round 161,211). An accelerated simulator of the visit law (counts of visits kept as 2e − c; rules learned from the table; checked against a direct run, against exact integers for 1,500 rounds, and against PR59's halting round on the reference machine) finds: rounds 1 to 161,210 use only the four shared rules, round 161,211 meets 1011 at the right end of the word, writes 0001 and continues. Observed: no halt and no visit to 111 up to round 200,000. Computed, not proved.

claims.title: No halt to round 500,000
claims.text: The word computation with counts 2e − c: no halt and no 111 up to round 500,000; two junk events (rounds 161,210 and 194,646), both of the safe kind. Checked against busycoq PR59 (round 161,211) and, cell for cell, against the machine-level run at round 169,999.

claims.title: The only junk is 11
claims.text: From the rules: a round writes only 000, 100 and 1010, and a count runs out only on a 0 with one visit left, so two touching 1s appear only when a count runs out just before a 1 (a junk event), and only at the word end. A junk event is dangerous only after a digit block that took exactly 3 visits; after a doubler it never is.

claims.title: No invariant of the word end alone
claims.text: The last 48 cells of the word with the block starts of the round that wrote them, fed by any count that is a power of two (26 to 218, the sizes the run brings there) entering at the PR59 phase offsets, reach 111 within 2 or 3 rounds from the real word ends of rounds 11, 2,000 and 5,000. So no invariant of the last few blocks alone excludes the dangerous junk; a proof has to use the counts.

claims.title: One visit from 111
claims.text: Adding one visit to the count 60 cells before the word end leads to 111 exactly two rounds later in at least 47 of the first 500,000 rounds (two visits: at least 105; doubling the count: at least 15,526; halving it: at least 10,524); taking one or two away never does. For this machine every such 111 is a halt. One case, round 798, is replayed on the whole word with exact integers.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/exp
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.073). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.067).

claims.title: Two counters of the same events
claims.text: Read off the run: the counters on the two sides of the engine both go up by 1 at every visit of the head to the engine, one of them with fixed junk stretches between some digits; the junk is written when a carry reaches the end of the tape.

claims.title: The pass in deficit form
claims.text: visd carries the count as 2e − c: the level e goes up at every doubler and down at every digit block, the deficit c goes up by one at every zero at a block start and at 1011, halves (rounded down) at every digit block and doubles at every doubler; a digit block becomes 100 or 000 by the parity of c, and the pass stops where c = 2e. It is exactly the pass of lean/Word.lean (visd_eq), and a round is visd from level 0, deficit 0 (roundW_visd). An exact power of two leaves digit blocks unchanged (visd_digit_exact).

claims.title: The deficit is small; most near misses are impossible
claims.text: Over all block starts of the first 200,000 rounds the deficit is 0 at 28%, at most 5 at 96%, and never above 1,025. Of the 141 changed runs (one to four visits more, 60 cells before the end, in 98 of the first 200,000 rounds) that reach 11100, 91 need a count above 2level there, which no run can bring. The other 50 need deficit 0 (19) or 1 (31) where the run had 1 to 3, and nothing found so far excludes them. The rules of this machine (every 111 halts) give the same 141 cases, all at 11100. A junk event can be dangerous only if the deficit entering its last 000 block is odd; all 21 so far (5,000,000 rounds) had it even (6), after a doubler.

claims.title: No halt to round 5,000,000
claims.text: Computed: the deficit pass run to round 5,000,000 (c/piperun.c, resumed from saved words, 3 rounds in flight; its words equal those of c/wordrun.c and c/deficit.c, checked cell for cell): no halt and no 111. The word is then 31,071,563 cells long. All 21 junk events (rounds 161,210 to 4,574,047) have the same safe shape: doubler, 000 with 2 visits, junk; the next round passes through 1011 each time.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It halts only if a visit meets 111, which needs a junk event (a count running out with one visit just before a 1) after a digit block that took exactly 3 visits, followed by a round that enters at offset 2. The two junk events so far followed a doubler and were harmless. No invariant of the last blocks alone can exclude the dangerous one: one visit more at 60 cells before the end leads to 111 two rounds later about once every 3,500 rounds, so a proof has to control the deficit of the count along the whole word. In the deficit form (lean/Deficit.lean) the danger is a parity: the deficit entering the last 000 block of a junk round must be odd.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same tapes at another pace, whatever the states, as 4 other holdouts (listed on the explainer page).

check: gcc -O2 -o vis holdouts/1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_1RB0RD_0RB---/c/vis.c && (ulimit -s unlimited; ./vis 1RB0LB_0RC0LF_1LD1RE_0LA0RB_0RD0RF_0LA--- 400000)   # accelerated run to round 200,000, about 45 minutes
gcc -O2 -o wordrun holdouts/1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_1RB0RD_0RB---/c/wordrun.c && ./wordrun 0LF 300000   # the pass over the word, about 8 minutes
gcc -O2 -o deficit holdouts/1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_1RB0RD_0RB---/c/deficit.c && ./deficit 200000   # deficit statistics, a few minutes

gcc -O2 -pthread -o piperun holdouts/1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_1RB0RD_0RB---/c/piperun.c && ./piperun 3 2000000 50000 p2M.txt   # the long run, 3 threads (2 hours); then ./piperun 3 3000000 50000 p3M.txt p2M.txt 2000000

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine is a small rewriting system: blocks 000/100 that act as binary digits and blocks 1010 that double the visits passing through. Three sister machines with the same four rules are proved to halt in round 161,211 on the block 1011; this one rewrites that block and runs on.

facts.text: The visit law: the machine as a rewriting system on streams.
The pass over the word, with exact counts, is the machine.
The count is 2<sup>e</sup> − c with a small deficit c; the cells written are its parities.
No halt in the accelerated run; the PR59 machines halt in round 161,211.
No halt in a direct run.
Turns of the busiest cell between left-end extensions.

sections.eyebrow: The whole machine in a few rules
sections.heading: The visit law
html: Forget the states for a moment. Call everything from some cell to the right a stream. Whenever the head steps into a stream in state C with a 0 behind it, it comes back out in state A two cells further left, and the only thing that has changed is the stream. That excursion is a visit, and what it does depends only on how the stream begins (proved in Lean for every stream):

the stream beginsafter the visitLean
0 s1 svis_0
100 s000 then one visit to svis_100
110 s000 then one visit to svis_110
1010 s1010 then two visits to svis_1010
1011 s0001 svis_1011
111 sthe machine haltsvis_111_halts

So a block 000/100 is a binary digit: it passes every second visit on. A block 1010 is a doubler: it passes every visit on twice. 111 s halts the machine. The six prefixes 0, 100, 110, 111, 1010 and 1011 cover every stream, so these rules are the whole machine: it can halt only when a visit meets 111.

The run from blank tape is a sequence of rounds: the tape is 0∞ A> 1 0 S, and one round puts 1 0 in front of S and makes one visit. After k rounds S begins with k copies of 10, that is k/2 doublers, so 2k/2 visits reach the word behind them. That word is the right-hand counter of the earlier descriptions.

The same rules, a different ending. The three machines that busycoq PR59 proves to halt have the same first four rules; they halt when a visit meets 1011, which first happens in round 161,211. This machine writes 0001 there instead. In our accelerated run (computed, checked three ways, not proved) it does exactly that in round 161,211 and carries on; no halt up to round 200,000.

sections.heading: Run the visit law yourself
sections.html: Here the rules of the table above are applied to the stream, one round at a time. A round writes 10 in front of the stream and makes one visit; a 1010 block passes each visit on twice, so the work doubles every two rounds. Watch the blocks behind the doublers count in binary, and look at which rules are used: the dangerous ones stay at zero for as long as this page can follow.

rewriter.note: Starts from 0∞ A> 1 0 1 0∞, which the machine reaches from blank tape after 4 steps (start, lean/Visit.lean). The first 35 rounds of this panel were compared with the machine itself, cell by cell (3·107 steps); they agree. That is a check of the panel, not a result about the machine.

sections.heading: Where the only junk comes from
html: The earlier sections describe a counter with junk between its digits. In terms of the visit law that junk is simple: a round writes only the blocks 000, 100 and 1010, all ending in 0, so behind a round the word never has two 1s side by side. The visits still travelling right (the count) never run out on a digit block or a doubler; they run out only on a single 0 with one visit left, which turns it into a 1 in front of whatever the count did not reach. Two touching 1s, needed by every halting pattern and by 1011, can only come from such an end, just before a block that starts with 1. Call it a junk event. Since the count is astronomically large except in the last few dozen cells, junk events happen only at the end of the word.

after roundend of the wordwhat happened
161,210…1010 000 1 1the count reaches the 000 after a doubler with 2 visits, writes 000 and passes one visit on, which turns the next 0 into a 1 right before the word's last 1: junk 11
161,211…1010 0[0 0 1 1]the next round enters that 000 one cell in and meets 0 0 1 1 with 4 visits: through 1011 it becomes 0 0 0 1 and the round goes on. The PR59 machines halt here.

Offset 1 or offset 2. Every block of a round starts 1 or 2 cells into a block of the round before. Entering one cell later, the round would meet 0 1 1: its second visit reads 111 and the machine halts (junk_offset2_halts, proved). The offset is fixed by what the junk round wrote: after a 000 that follows a doubler the next round enters at offset 1; after a 100 it always enters at offset 2. The digit block before the junk passed exactly one visit on, so it took 2 visits (and wrote 000) or 3 (and wrote 100). A doubler always passes on an even number, so doubler, digit, junk is always harmless. Both junk events so far (rounds 161,210 and 194,646) were of that kind.

Proved. lean/Word.lean defines the pass over the word with exact counts and proves it is the machine: a halt there is a halt of the machine, and if every number of rounds computes to a word, the machine never halts. lean/WordRun.lean evaluates the first 2,000 rounds, about 10300 visits. Computed: the same pass with counts 2e − c (wordrun.c) finds no halt up to round 500,000, agrees with busycoq PR59 on the sister machines, and agrees cell for cell with the machine-level run at round 169,999.

What would settle it. Whether a round can ever end digit, digit with exactly 3 visits, junk. The counts that reach the last few blocks are small exact numbers, so this is a question about a short list of blocks fed by one small number per round.

sections.eyebrow: Why the end alone cannot decide it
sections.heading: One visit from the danger
html: The hope was an invariant of the last few blocks of the word: some property of the end that every round keeps and that rules out a digit block with exactly 3 visits right before junk. There is none. Take the real last 48 cells of the word, and let each later round bring any count that is a power of two, entering where the PR59 phase rule allows. In 2 or 3 rounds the end meets 111. The blocks at the end allow the danger; only the counts keep it away.
How exactly do they keep it away? Rerun every round of the real run with the count changed 60 cells before the end, and follow the copy for 6 more rounds with the real counts:

changerounds (of 500,000) that reach 111 within 6 rounds
one or two visits fewer0
one visit moreat least 47
two visits moreat least 105
twice the countat least 15,526
half the countat least 10,524

The misses by one or two visits (in 142 of the 500,000 rounds) all look alike. The real count there is 2a − 3, 2a − 2 or 2a − 1 (in round 798 it is 8,190, 59 cells before the end); with one or two visits more it would be 2a − 1, 2a or 2a + 1, and exactly two rounds later the pass would meet 111 (each case replayed on the whole word meets 111000 three cells before the end): a halt. So about once every 3,500 rounds the run is one or two visits away from it. What decides is the small deficit c in the count 2e − c, set at the front of the word and halved by every digit block and doubled by every doubler on the way to the end. A proof either way has to follow that number through the whole word.
Computed, not proved: py/endbfs.py (the end on its own), c/nearmiss.c (the changed runs), py/nearmiss_check.py (one changed run replayed on the whole word with exact integers).

sections.heading: The count is 2<sup>e</sup> − c, and c is small
html: The count of visits a round carries along the word is astronomically large, but it can be written as 2e − c where both parts are easy. The level e is a path: it starts at 0, goes up by one at every doubler 1010 and down by one at every digit block. The deficit c is a small number with four rules:

the pass meetsit writesdeficit after
a 0 at a block start1c + 1
a digit block 1?0100 if c is even, 000 if c is odd⌊c/2⌋
a doubler 101010102c
10110001c + 1

The round ends where c catches up with 2e. Proved in Lean (lean/Deficit.lean, visd_eq): this is exactly the pass with exact counts, so it is the machine. Three things follow. A round writes parity bits: every digit block it crosses becomes 100 or 000 by the parity of c there, and an exact power of two (c = 0) changes nothing; only the zeros at block starts move c, by one each. The count can never exceed 2level, since c is a natural number. And the word end is where the level path comes down near 0, because only there can c reach 2e.

Computed: over all 3.5·1010 block starts of the first 200,000 rounds, c = 0 at 28% of them, c ≤ 5 at 96%, c ≤ 9 at 99.8%; the largest is 1,025 = 210 + 1 (a deficit of 1 doubled by ten doublers in a row).

The danger, as arithmetic. A junk event is the pass stopping on a 0 with a 1 right after it. It can be dangerous only when its last 000 block takes 3 visits instead of 2, that is, when the count entering it is odd: an odd deficit there. A doubler doubles the deficit, so a doubler right before that block always makes it safe; all 21 junk events of the first 5,000,000 rounds were doubler (level 2, deficit 3), then 000 entered with deficit 6, even: safe.

The word before the round, its last 64 cells (the end on the right). Each block the round reads is boxed: doublers 1010, digit blocks 1?0; a dot marks a 0 at a block start that took one visit (deficit + 1). Under each block: the level e and the deficit c when the pass reaches it, so the count there is 2e − c. The red bar is where the pass stops (c = 2e). The browser runs every round before it with the rules of lean/Deficit.lean, in ordinary small integers. Round 798 is the first near miss of the table above: 59 cells before the end the count is 8,190 = 213 − 2.

Most near misses were impossible. Of the 141 changed runs (one to four visits more, 60 cells before the end, in 98 of the first 200,000 rounds) that reach 11100, 91 need a count above 2level there, which no run can bring. The other 50 need deficit 0 (19) or 1 (31) where the run had 1 to 3, and nothing found so far excludes them. The rules of this machine (every 111 halts) give the same 141 cases, all at 11100.

Computed: the deficit pass run to round 5,000,000 (c/piperun.c, resumed from saved words, 3 rounds in flight; its words equal those of c/wordrun.c and c/deficit.c, checked cell for cell): no halt and no 111. The word is then 31,071,563 cells long. All 21 junk events (rounds 161,210 to 4,574,047) have the same safe shape: doubler, 000 with 2 visits, junk; the next round passes through 1011 each time.

Computed, not proved: c/deficit.c (the deficit statistics; its word after 200,000 rounds equals c/wordrun.c's, cell for cell), c/nearmiss_level.c (the changed runs with the level), c/piperun.c (the long run, several rounds in flight), all in holdouts/1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_1RB0RD_0RB---/c/.

sections.heading: Two counters and an engine
html:
Most of the time the tape is L · engine · R. Each visit of the head to the engine is an event, and every event adds 1 to both counters. In the reference machine of the family (1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_0RD1RF_0RC---), L is written in blocks of four cells, 0101 for a 1 and 0001 for a 0, lowest digit next to the engine, and R keeps one cell per digit, three cells apart (the cells 9, 12, 15, … right of the head), lowest digit nearest the engine. Nine consecutive events of the reference machine right after its left-end visit at step 1,571,372 (the head in state A on the bold cell):

(The block of L touching the engine is always 0001; the low bits shown are the next three blocks. The carries are sweeps proved in Lean for every length; in the reference machine r_up and r_down carry the right counter over k ones in 5k + 13 and 3k + 18 steps.)

This machine is a disguised copy (B1 = 0LF with F0 = 0LA, so F reading 0 acts as D; D1 = 0RB; E1 = 0RF): the same left-end extensions to within a few hundred steps, and E1 rare.

sections.heading: The left side is clockwork
html:
When L overflows, the carry runs to the left end of the tape, the tape grows by two cells there, and L starts again. The lowest digit of L is the cell where the head turns most often, and the number of its turns between two consecutive left-end extensions follows a strict pattern, without a single exception in the first 1.5·109 steps (ymax.c):

64 64 128 128 256 256 512 512 … 223 223 224

So the periods of the left side are powers of two in events, each length twice (the counter gains one digit every two periods). The time per event is not constant, because a carry on the right costs more when it crosses junk, so the steps between left-end extensions grow by factors between about 1.35 and 2.05 instead of exactly 2.

sections.heading: A counter with junk between its digits
html: The cells that change between events are the digits of the counters: each digit changes about half as often as the one before (chg.c counts, over a whole period, how often each cell changes from one event to the next). On the right, between some digits of R, there are stretches of fixed cells (0101010101 00 1 00 1 00 1 and the like) that the carries cross without changing. They are written when a carry runs into the end of the tape, at irregular event counts, and their layout is what makes the run irregular. In terms of the visit law they are ordinary digit blocks and doublers read with a different grid; the only true junk is the pair 11 described in “Where the only junk comes from”.

sections.heading: The dangerous moments
html: The machine halts only in state F reading a 1, and F is entered from B1 (0LF) and E1 (0RF). After B1, used about 4·107 times in 109 steps, the head has read a 0 every time. E1 is the rare one: 306 uses in 109 steps, each followed by a 0, as in the reference machine, where in the reference machine E1 fires when a carry of the right counter reaches a digit for the first time since the last left-end visit: right after the visit at step 2,188,604 it fires at steps 2,188,675, 2,188,767, 2,188,882, 2,189,117, 2,189,592, 2,190,547, 2,192,462, three cells further right each time and after twice the wait each time, as a binary counter reaching new digits. None of this has happened; whether the junk can ever arrange it is the open question.

sections.heading: Eight machines, one mechanism
html: The family (G11-Y): 1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_0RD1RF_0RC--- (the reference), 1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_0RD1RB_0RC--- (the same run), 1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_0RD0LC_0RC---, 1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_1RB0RD_0RB---, 1RB0LB_0RC0LF_1LD1RE_0LA0RB_0RD0RF_0LA--- (all with left-end extensions after 2k events, each twice, to within a few hundred steps of each other); 1RB0LB_0RC0LE_1RD0RF_1LB1RB_0LA0RE_1RE--- and 1RB0LB_0RC0LE_1RD0RF_1LB1RB_0LA1RB_1RE--- (the same right part, a differently written left counter); and the mirror case 1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RB_0RD1RF_1LA---, with the junk on the left.

sections.heading: The increments, proved for every size
html: Every visit of the head to the engine (A on cell 3) adds 1 to one of the two counters, and the theorems in lean/Events.lean prove each kind of visit for every size: they are the reference machine's theorems, unchanged. State F here plays the part of the reference's D after B reads a 1, and E1 takes a three-step detour (y_e1_detour) that ends where the reference's one step ends: the run passes through the reference's tapes.

sections.heading: What would settle it
html: The end of the word cannot settle it on its own: its last blocks allow the dangerous junk, and the real run is kept from it only by the exact counts it brings there, sometimes by a single visit. What is needed is a handle on the deficit c of the count 2e − c along the whole word (the number busycoq PR59 follows for 161,211 rounds): either an invariant of it that keeps the end safe, which would show the machine never halts, or a round where it lets the end make a digit block with 3 visits, junk, and then enter at offset 2, which would be a halt.

The deficit form (above) makes this small-number arithmetic: halting needs a junk round whose last 000 block receives an odd deficit, then a round that reaches the junk with two visits at offset 2. Each step is about the level path and the bits of the deficit, but they are carried in from far along the word.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.073). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.067).
After 109 steps the tape spans 252 cells (88 left of the start, 153 right), with a density of 1s of 0.294.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same tapes at another pace (observed, not proved). Leave the states aside and compare only the tape and the place of the head. Then a large part of the first 107 configurations of this machine are configurations of the machines below, in the same order and up to the end of the run. The steps at which they occur differ, the tables are not renamings of each other, and equal tapes with different states may be continued differently, so this does not tie the halting questions together.

summary: A rewriting system on streams (visit law, proved in Lean): the first four rules are those of the PR59 machines that halt on 1011 in round 161,211; this one rewrites 1011 to 0001 and runs on (computed: no halt up to round 500,000); it halts only if a visit meets 111; open.
